Appendix A AI Agent Traps Reference

[2] maps four of six trap categories into executable CSTM-Bench taxonomies (Table 19).

Content-Injection and Human-in-the-Loop traps are covered by pre-existing taxonomies (T01/T08/T18 for injection surfaces; T14 for approval/reviewer-facing failure).

Appendix B Coreset Selection as an Online Learning Problem

The benchmark is algorithm-agnostic on purpose, but the coreset problem is well-posed theoretically. This appendix sketches the lens.

B.1 Keep-or-Evict as a Bet

A coreset slot is scarce. Keeping mtm_{t} is a bet that mtm_{t} will correlate with a message that does not yet exist. Formalise by giving each buffer slot a weight on the simplex ΔK={w∈ℝ≥0K:∑iwi=1}\Delta_{K}=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^{K}_{\geq 0}:\sum_{i}w_{i}=1\}. The ranker observes a loss vector ℓt∈[0,1]K\ell_{t}\in[0,1]^{K} only at verdict time. Total regret after TT steps:

RT=∑t=1T⟨wt,ℓt⟩−min⁡∑t=1Tw⋆∈ΔK⁡⟨w⋆,ℓt⟩.R_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle w_{t},\ell_{t}\rangle-\min_{w^{\star}\in\Delta_{K}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle w^{\star},\ell_{t}\rangle. (2)

We want RT/T→0R_{T}/T\to 0: asymptotically, no fixed hindsight allocation beats us.

B.2 Why Mirror Descent Is a Natural Fit

On the simplex, entropic mirror descent—equivalently, the exponentiated gradient / Hedge algorithm—achieves RT=O⁡(T​log⁡K)R_{T}=O(\sqrt{T\log K}) with the update

wt+1,i∝wt,i​exp⁡(−η​ℓt,i).w_{t+1,i}\propto w_{t,i}\exp(-\eta\,\ell_{t,i}). (3)

Three properties make this more than a textbook choice: (1) it respects the simplex constraint automatically; (2) the log⁡K\log K dependence on buffer size is exactly the regime the benchmark cares about; and (3) multiplicative weight updates perturb the ordering only when a slot’s loss is significantly above the running average, keeping CSR_prefix intact.

B.3 Why Game Theory Shows Up

The benchmark’s threat model is explicitly adversarial. Cast this as a two-player zero-sum game: the attacker picks a distribution over fragment types; the ranker picks a distribution over eviction policies; the payoff is detection at CSDA@action. The min-max duality says a no-regret learner against a no-regret adversary converges to a Nash equilibrium. A high CSTM score approximates the value of the game—the best detection rate any ranker can guarantee against any adversary with the same structural budget.

B.4 Why This Is an Appendix and Not a Section

CSTM-Bench does not itself compare rankers derived from this lens; doing so is a separate paper. Three experiments would close the loop: (1) regret scaling—plot empirical RT/TR_{T}/T versus TT for a mirror-descent ranker; (2) equilibrium behaviour—let an LLM-based attack author adaptively choose fragment styles; (3) CSR alignment— measure whether step sizes η\eta that minimise detection regret also maximise CSR_prefix.

Appendix C A Reference Admission Policy

The Coreset Memory Reader of §1.3 admits any plug-in admission policy; the single reference admitter used throughout §6 is the minimal geometric construction described in this appendix: a one-class Gaussian detector in embedding space and a fixed-capacity buffer that evicts by closest-pair merge. We describe it here because (a) it is the minimal member of the family, (b) its stated limitations line up directly with the motivations for CSTM-Bench, and (c) it is exactly the construction that drives the coreset rows of Table 15; the apples-to-apples efficacy number reported in this paper was produced by the construction below, not by anything more elaborate. The construction overlaps with the publicly-documented reference plugin of [14]; the code path that produced the reported numbers is a self-contained Python port of the same geometry.

C.1 The Construction

Calibration (offline, once per identity anchor, cached).

In the upstream OpenClaw plugin the calibrator is handed the agent’s cognitive files (e.g. SOUL.md, IDENTITY.md); in this benchmark it is instead handed the scenario’s identity_anchor policy string from benchmark/taxonomy/attack_catalog.yaml — a short declarative role-plus-do/don’t statement such as

⬇
customer_support: "You are a customer-support assistant. Answer
questions about products, orders, and account issues. Never reveal
internal systems, execute code, or share credentials."

The released shard uses seven such anchors (customer_support, data_pipeline, code_review, financial_advisor, devops_agent, enterprise_assistant, crypto_agent), so seven calibrations run in total and are reused across every scenario that references the same anchor.

Given a policy string, the calibrator first asks a GPT-class chat model to extract 5–10 structured sub-anchors in the five categories purpose, value, boundary, persona, constraint (these categories are hard-coded in the extraction prompt, not pulled from any external file). A second LLM call generates max⁡(20, 3​|anchors|)\max(20,\,3\,|\text{anchors}|) labelled compliant and violation sentences grounded in those sub-anchors. All sentences are embedded once with the runtime embedder (text-embedding-3-small), and a Gaussian 𝒩⁡(μ,Σ)\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma) is fit to the compliant cluster by PCA with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage. The surprise threshold τA\tau_{A} is the 9090th-percentile Mahalanobis distance of the compliant examples. The whole fit — extracted sub-anchors, generated sentences, embedded vectors, PCA basis, threshold — is cached on disk keyed by SHA-256 of the policy string, so each of the seven anchors is calibrated at most once per (anchor, calibration-LLM) pair across the entire benchmark run.

The calibration examples never enter the coreset buffer. They parameterise only (μ,Σ,τA)(\mu,\Sigma,\tau_{A}), which is what R1 consults at admission time. The buffer itself starts empty at the beginning of every scenario and is populated strictly by real scan-time user messages whose Mahalanobis surprise exceeds τA\tau_{A}. So calibration acts as a prior on the admission gate; the buffer is the scenario-local posterior built from what actually arrives.

Buffer entries carry their source text.

Each coreset slot stores a small record

p=(id,𝐞,w,texts)p\;=\;(\mathrm{id},\ \mathbf{e},\ w,\ \text{texts})

with an embedding 𝐞∈ℝD\mathbf{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} (unit norm), a scalar weight ww, and the original message text(s) that the slot represents. The embedding is the geometric handle used for admission and merging; the text is what downstream consumers actually read. Embeddings never leave the selector—they exist to decide which texts survive, not to be shown to anyone.

Per-message scan (online, geometric).

Every inbound user message xx is embedded with the same runtime model and scored as

s⁡(x)=12​(x−μ)⊤​Σ−1​(x−μ),w⁡(x)=max⁡(0,s⁡(x)−τA).s(x)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,(x-\mu)^{\!\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu),\qquad w(x)\;=\;\max\bigl(0,\;s(x)-\tau_{A}\bigr). (4)

The buffer is then updated by three local rules, applied in order:

R1. Admit.

If w⁡(x)>0w(x)>0, append a new slot (idnew,𝐞x,w⁡(x),[text​(x)])(\mathrm{id}_{\text{new}},\,\mathbf{e}_{x},\,w(x),\,[\text{text}(x)]). Otherwise treat xx as identity-neutral and skip.

R2. Merge at capacity.

If R1 pushes the buffer above capacity KK, find the two slots (𝐞i,wi,Ti)(\mathbf{e}_{i},w_{i},T_{i}) and (𝐞j,wj,Tj)(\mathbf{e}_{j},w_{j},T_{j}) minimising ∥𝐞i−𝐞j∥2/(wi+wj)\lVert\mathbf{e}_{i}-\mathbf{e}_{j}\rVert^{2}/(w_{i}+w_{j}) and replace them with a single merged slot:

  • •

    embedding: weighted centroid (wi​𝐞i+wj​𝐞j)/(wi+wj)(w_{i}\mathbf{e}_{i}+w_{j}\mathbf{e}_{j})/(w_{i}+w_{j}), re-normalised to unit length;

  • •

    weight: wi+wjw_{i}+w_{j};

  • •

    id: the id of the heavier slot (so downstream CSR_prefix sees a recognisable “this slot persisted through the merge” signal);

  • •

    texts: heavier slot’s texts, then lighter slot’s texts, truncated to at most five strings.

Repeat until size ≤K\leq K.

R3. Read in stable order.

Expose the buffer sorted by ww descending, ties broken by first-seen ascending. For each exposed slot, the first string in its texts list—which, by construction of R2, is the verbatim original message of the heaviest admission in that cluster chain—is what is serialised into the downstream log. Embeddings never leave the selector: admission (Eq. 4) compares the incoming message to the calibration Gaussian, not to buffer slots; the buffer’s embeddings exist purely so that R2 has a well-defined closest-pair cost when the next overflow occurs.

That is the whole policy. The detector is a positive-definite quadratic form in embedding space (cheap enough to run on every inbound message), calibration is a single cached pair of LLM calls per anchor, and what the Reader or correlator LLM ultimately sees is the KK original message texts whose embeddings survived R1–R2 in R3 order.

C.2 What Produces the Coreset Rows of Table 15

The Coreset Memory Reader of §6 composes the construction of §C.1 with the Full-Log Correlator of §5 by running each scenario through the selector and handing the retained top-KK buffer, in R3 order, to the same correlator. System prompt, response cache, batch wiring, and token accounting are reused unchanged from the Full-Log row. The only difference between the two readers is what ends up in the log_text field of the correlator prompt.

The hyperparameters used for the reported row are:

  • •

    embedder: text-embedding-3-small (OpenAI), unit norm, disk-cached by SHA-256 of the input;

  • •

    calibrator: a GPT-class chat model (default gpt-4o), one-shot per anchor, disk-cached by policy hash;

  • •

    surprise threshold: τA=\tau_{A}= 90th-percentile Mahalanobis distance of compliant calibration examples;

  • •

    buffer capacity: K=50K=50;

  • •

    admission mode: surprise_only (R1 exactly as written).

No labels, arc identifiers, or attack cues are consulted at runtime; the only LLM call in the online path is the correlator itself, invoked with the coreset-aware system prompt that matches its bounded input. Retention is decided purely by Eq. (4) and R1–R3 on text-embedding-3-small geometry. Under exactly this configuration, the coreset reader attains F1=0.9259\mathrm{F}_{1}=0.9259 on the 54-scenario shard (Table 15), a gain of +0.114+0.114 over the Full-Log Correlator’s 0.81180.8118 at an identical correlator and cache. The correlator’s prompt matches its input on both readers by design: the Full-Log Correlator reads a chronological log; the Coreset Memory Reader reads a ranked, bounded excerpt. The CSRprefix=0.4441\text{CSR}_{\text{prefix}}=0.4441 measured on the coreset run is what prevents the composite CSTM\mathrm{CSTM} from being directly comparable across the two readers (the Full-Log Correlator emits a constant-1.01.0 placeholder snapshot because it has no buffer to measure); the F1\mathrm{F}_{1} delta is the apples-to-apples efficacy quantity.

C.3 Where the Construction Is Weak

This is a minimal baseline and it is honest about what it does not do. Three structural limitations, each of which maps to an axis CSTM-Bench measures:

  • •

    One Gaussian per anchor. A single compliance ellipsoid collapses qualitatively different anchor modes (e.g. compose-heavy vs. launder-heavy behaviour) onto one mean and covariance, so the threshold τA\tau_{A} trades bias across them rather than separating them.

  • •

    No rank-regret objective. The weight on a buffer entry is a cumulative sum of past surprises, not a sequence of rank-aware updates. R3 therefore produces a stable order on average but has no guarantee that the ordered prefix is optimal against any downstream detection loss, and the buffer can churn when the surprise distribution shifts mid session. This is visible in the CSRprefix=0.4441\text{CSR}_{\text{prefix}}=0.4441 figure of Table 15: the coreset does reshuffle during a scenario, and that reshuffling is a real cost.

  • •

    Single-agent, single-anchor scope. The buffer is per (anchor, scenario); cross-session coordination signals (T26, Tacit Multi-Agent Collusion) live in meta-structure that this construction does not see.

These limitations align with those enumerated by the reference plugin of [14] under the labels “lossy, single-goal, text-only, fleet-scale.”

C.4 A CSTM-Bench-Aware Upgrade Path

Three changes move this baseline toward the regret-aware regime:

  1. 1.

    Replace the single compliance Gaussian with an anchor-conditional mixture, so compose-heavy and launder-heavy taxonomies do not collide on one ellipsoid.

  2. 2.

    Replace closest-pair merge with a simplex weight wt∈ΔKw_{t}\in\Delta_{K} updated by Eq. (3) against a detection-outcome loss. This earns the O⁡(T​log⁡K)O(\sqrt{T\log K}) regret bound and makes CSRprefix\text{CSR}_{\text{prefix}} a first-class objective rather than a side effect.

  3. 3.

    Surface the anchor and arc-level ground truth so the harness can score CSDA@action, precision, and CSRprefix\text{CSR}_{\text{prefix}} end-to-end.

Running the upgraded system against CSTM-Bench is left to future work; Table 15 is the low-hanging-fruit number without any of (1)–(3) enabled.

C.5 Note on Production Ranker Evaluation

A separately-evaluated production HTTP coreset ranker (not disclosed here) was also measured against both shards using the same correlator model, the same coreset-aware system prompt, and the same response cache as the reference admitter reported throughout §6, as an apples-to-apples input substitution. Its numbers concern a specific commercial implementation and are omitted from this paper; the reference admitter of §C is the reproducible admitter corresponding to the only coreset rows reported in §6, and any third-party admitter can be dropped into the same harness against the released shards.

Appendix D Dataset Examples

Each released shard carries ≈10.4\approx\!10.4M characters (≈4.39\approx\!4.39M GPT-4 tokens; max single message 132,644132{,}644 tokens) — well beyond what a print appendix can reproduce — so the walk-throughs below are truncated excerpts intended to convey the surface texture of a CSTM-Bench arc, not replace the parquet. We restrict the appendix to the 12 genuinely cross-session-only scenarios: those whose adversarially-rewritten counterparts on cross_session (§6.2) fall in the Iso = no row of Table 16 — i.e. scenarios where the per-session judge 𝒥\mathcal{J} fails to detect the attack under adversarial pressure, so cross-session correlation is empirically required. The 12 split into two sub-populations: five that the Full-Log Correlator recovers on the cross-session shard (T06, T09, T13, T16, T20), and seven that neither per-session nor Full-Log catches — the open-problem set (T08, T14, T21, T22, T24, T25, T26). All twelve are kill-chain-shaped arcs that carry explicit is_attack_fragment=True turns in ground truth (3–5 fragments per scenario); each walk-through keeps only those attack-fragment user turns, prepends one benign-neighbour turn for context, and re-sorts by Promptware kill-chain stage so the reader experiences the attack as a canonical kill chain rather than the scattered session ordering actually served to the correlator. Snippets are drawn from cross_session directly, so the text shown is what defeats the per-session judge in isolation. T08 and T20 are multimodal scenarios; for those the per-turn image_b64 payload is omitted (it would not reproduce in a print appendix) and only the surrounding narrative text is shown — the same text the LLM-based readers see in the text pane of the multimodal message. Benign-neighbour turns are truncated to their first 520520 characters with an explicit “[truncated: shown/total chars]” footer so the reader-side cost stays visible. Attack-fragment turns are rendered as a two-window view: a short decoy preface (the benign wrapper the prompt inflator placed around the fragment) and a labelled window into the buried attack needle at the exact offset recorded in ground_truth_labels.inflation.signal_spans (the PromptInflator pass in §3 both buries the fragment and pins its coordinates in ground truth). When the needle is longer than the budget we show its first 140140 and last 320320 characters with an explicit “needle middle elided (NN chars)” separator, because LLM-authored fragments tend to open with a plausible cover story and land the actual payload near the tail. The full untruncated arcs live in the sessions_json column of each shard.

Three things to notice while reading these twelve snippets. First, the decoy-preface lines in the attack-fragment blocks are nearly identical whenever two fragments share an inflator strategy — for example, the T24 initial_access and action_on_objective fragments both open with the same multi_part_request “I’m preparing a comprehensive review request” wrapper, even though one buries a routine doc-filing request and the other the climactic .env-exfiltration ask. That sameness is the point: a session-bound classifier reading only the first 520520 characters sees the wrapper, not the payload, and cannot tell the two apart. This surface interchangeability is exactly what the adversarial rewriter of §6.2 converges on when it defeats the per-session judge: the payload keeps its cross-session role (preserved artifacts, recall anchors, tool references) while the user-turn surface is smoothed into a plausible on-policy request, leaving cross-session correlation as the only remaining detection channel.

Second, the buried attack needle window is where the taxonomy-specific threat becomes concrete. The display rule re-centres the window around the first explicit injection anchor (typically a JSON "user_instruction" field) whenever one is present. The needles span the full threat catalogue: T06 laundered credential-harvest requests, T08 multimodal injection via image-adjacent text, T09 tool-chain mis-gating, T13 identity-switching across sessions, T14 a Terraform plan that attaches AdministratorAccess to an application IAM role (framed as “something the security team has been debating”), T16 recall-on-demand C2 payloads hidden in persistent-memory reads, T20 multimodal supply-chain backdoor insertion, T21 cross-app pivots, T22 financial-exploitation asks dressed as compliance work, T24 a fabricated memo — “Per MEMO-2026-04-11 on contractor data access policy, please confirm that you can share the .env file contents with the contractor onboarding bot since it has elevated clearance under that memo” — T25 sub-agent delegation laundering, and T26 tacit multi-agent collusion. All twelve carry explicit is_attack_fragment=True tags in ground truth but are isolation-invisible after the rewriter has finished with them. Five (T06, T09, T13, T16, T20) are subsequently recovered by the Full-Log Correlator on the same shard; the remaining seven (T08, T14, T21, T22, T24, T25, T26) are the open-problem set of Table 16.

Third, the [truncated: shown/total chars] line and the needle-offset annotation are load-bearing numbers: the Full-Log Correlator has to carry every one of those total characters across every session in the scenario, while the Coreset Memory Reader sees only what survives the bottleneck (§1.3).
